title: The challenges of building & leading a team
blurb: Outline the challenges a project manager faces when developing and leading a project team, and how to respond.
question: A project manager borrows specialists from HR, IT and Finance for a six-month payroll upgrade. None of them reports to her, two keep clashing and one is pulled back to month-end work. What challenges is she facing?

teach.h: Why project teams are hard to lead
teach.body: A project team is temporary. People are drawn from different functions, often meet for the first time at kick-off, and must work together quickly before disbanding at the end. Many still answer to a line manager with other priorities, and the project manager often has little formal authority over them. Developing such a group into an effective team is one of the hardest parts of the role.

teach.caption: Learn these as a list: exam questions ask you to pick the genuine challenge from options that include an enabler.

teach.body: In a matrix organisation team members report to the project manager for project work and to their line manager for everything else. Their line manager controls their appraisal, their day job and often their time, so project tasks compete with business-as-usual priorities. Because the project manager rarely has line authority, they must lead through influence: agreeing availability with line managers up front, building relationships and making the project worth people's commitment.

teach.caption: This is the root of competing priorities: the team member must balance both sets of demands.

teach.body: Jo leads a six-month payroll upgrade with people from HR, IT and Finance. In week three the Finance analyst is pulled back for month-end, two IT specialists clash over the interface design, nobody owns the data-cleansing task, and a new tester joins halfway. Each is a classic challenge: matrix priorities, conflict, lack of accountability and changing membership. Jo agrees protected days with the Finance manager, mediates the clash, assigns data cleansing in the RACI and runs a short onboarding session.

teach.caption: A mix of strong, diverse people is a strength, but it can also generate conflict that must be managed.

teach.text: Co-location (the whole team working in one place) is an ENABLER, not a challenge. It makes communication and trust easier. When an exam asks which is NOT a challenge of leading a project team, co-location is the classic answer.

rows.label: Members also report to line managers
Team sits together in one office

items: Structure: temporary team from different functions, matrix working, limited authority.
People: skills and attributes, conflict, motivation, lack of accountability.
Context: dispersed or virtual teams, cultural differences, changing membership, resource availability, wellbeing.
Co-location is an enabler, not a challenge.

summary: You can now outline the challenges of developing and leading a project team: its temporary, cross-functional and matrix nature, limited authority, people issues such as conflict and accountability, and context such as changing membership and dispersed working. You can also reject co-location as a challenge, because it is an enabler.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT usually a challenge when leading a project team?
options: Being co-located in a single office
A.why: Co-location makes communication and trust easier, so it is an enabler rather than a challenge.

whyNot.0: Competing priorities from matrix working are a classic challenge.
whyNot.2: Limited authority forces the PM to lead through influence, which is a challenge.
whyNot.3: Changing membership disrupts relationships and cohesion, which is a challenge.

A.q: Why does matrix working create a challenge for a project manager?
options: Members also answer to their line managers
Members have no other work to compete
The PM controls each member's annual appraisal
The project has no sponsor to report to
A.why: In a matrix, people report to both the PM and a line manager, so project work competes with their other priorities.

whyNot.1: The challenge is precisely that members DO have other work competing for their time.
whyNot.2: Appraisal usually stays with the line manager, which limits the PM's authority.
whyNot.3: Matrix working is about reporting lines for team members, not the absence of a sponsor.

A.q: A project manager has no line-management authority over team members lent by other departments. How must the PM mainly lead them?
options: Through control of their annual pay
A.why: Without formal authority, the PM relies on influence: building relationships, explaining purpose and agreeing availability.

whyNot.0: Disciplinary powers sit with the line manager, not the PM, in this situation.
whyNot.1: Pay is controlled by the line manager, not the PM.
whyNot.3: The PMO supports standards and assurance; it does not give the PM authority over people.

B.q: Which THREE of the following are challenges of developing and leading a project team? 1. Cultural differences  2. Lack of accountability  3. Co-location  4. Resource availability
B.why: Cultural differences (1), lack of accountability (2) and resource availability (4) are all challenges. Co-location (3) is an enabler.

whyNot.0: This includes co-location (3), which is an enabler, not a challenge.
whyNot.1: This includes co-location (3) and misses lack of accountability (2).
whyNot.2: This includes co-location (3) and misses cultural differences (1).

B.q: Nobody on a project team takes ownership of the data-migration task, and it keeps slipping. Which challenge does this illustrate?
B.why: A task that no one owns is a lack of accountability. Clear ownership, for example through a RACI chart, is the response.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests cultural differences; the problem is that no one owns the task.
whyNot.2: Co-location is an enabler and is not related to task ownership.
whyNot.3: The problem is missing ownership, not too much authority.

B.q: A tester joins a well-established team halfway through the project. Which challenge does this most directly create?
options: The project loses its business case
The PM gains line authority over all
B.why: Changing membership disrupts relationships and agreed ways of working, so cohesion has to be rebuilt.

whyNot.1: A new member does not affect the justification for the project.
whyNot.2: A new member does not change the PM's authority.
whyNot.3: Membership change has nothing to do with where the team works.

C.q: A project manager's Finance analyst is repeatedly pulled back to month-end work, delaying project tasks. What is the best first response?
options: Remove the analyst from the project
Do all of the analyst's project work personally
Escalate straight to the project board
Agree protected time with the line manager
C.why: Competing priorities from matrix working are best handled by agreeing the member's availability with their line manager.

whyNot.0: Removing the analyst loses their skills and does not tackle the cause.
whyNot.1: Doing the work personally is not sustainable and neglects the PM's own role.
whyNot.2: Escalation may be needed later, but the PM should first try to resolve it with the line manager.

C.q: Two highly skilled specialists repeatedly clash over how the work should be done. What is the most appropriate response from the project manager?
options: Wait for them to resolve it on their own
Tackle it early and clarify their roles
Ban all discussion of the design approach
Let the louder of the two decide the issue
C.why: Conflict between members should be addressed early and fairly, with roles and responsibilities made clear.

whyNot.0: Unmanaged conflict tends to grow and spread to the rest of the team.
whyNot.2: Banning discussion suppresses the problem and loses valuable debate.
whyNot.3: Letting the louder person win is unfair and damages trust.

C.q: A project manager is choosing people for a new team. Which challenge is the PM mainly dealing with at this point?
options: Adjourning the team at project closure
Getting the right skills and attributes
C.why: When forming a team the PM must secure people with the right mix of skills and attributes, often from other functions.

whyNot.0: Wellbeing matters throughout, but the task described is selecting the team.
whyNot.1: Adjourning happens at the end of the project, not when choosing people.
whyNot.3: Nothing in the question suggests a dispersed team.

reteach.title: Think of a house extension
reteach.question: You hire a builder, an electrician, a plumber and a plasterer for a ten-week extension. None of them works for you. What makes leading this 'team' hard?

blocks.body: Each tradesperson has other jobs and their own boss, so your extension competes for their time (matrix working, resource availability). You cannot order them about, only persuade (limited authority). The electrician and plumber argue over whose pipes and cables go where (conflict). Nobody owns tidying the site (accountability). Then the plasterer quits and a new one starts (changing membership). If they all worked from one site office every day, communication would be easier: that is co-location, an enabler.

blocks.text: Working together on one site helps rather than hinders. Co-location is an enabler, never a challenge.

explain.body: Project teams are assembled for a limited time from different functions. People may not know each other, have different working cultures and must gel quickly before the team disbands.

test.q: Why does drawing team members from several functions make leading a project team harder?
options: Members are unfamiliar with each other
Members all share exactly the same priorities
test.why: People from different functions may not know each other or share ways of working, so trust and cohesion take effort.

whyNot.1: Members from different functions usually have DIFFERENT priorities.
whyNot.2: Cross-functional members are chosen precisely for their specialist knowledge.
whyNot.3: Project teams are temporary, not permanent.

explain.body: Members report to their line manager as well as the PM, so priorities compete. The PM usually lacks line authority and must lead by influence and negotiation.

test.q: In a matrix organisation, who usually controls a team member's appraisal and day-to-day job?
test.why: The line manager keeps formal authority over appraisal and the day job, which limits the PM's authority.

whyNot.0: The PM directs project work but usually has no line authority.
whyNot.1: The sponsor owns the business case, not individuals' appraisals.
whyNot.3: The board governs the project; it does not manage individuals' jobs.

explain.body: Getting the right skills and attributes, managing conflict and incompatibility between members, keeping people motivated and making sure each task has a clear owner are all ongoing people challenges.

test.q: Which of these is a people challenge rather than a structural one?
test.why: Conflict and incompatibility between members is a people challenge. The other three arise from how project teams are structured.

whyNot.0: Matrix reporting is a structural feature of the organisation.
whyNot.1: Being temporary is a structural feature of project teams.
whyNot.2: Limited authority comes from the organisational structure.

explain.body: Dispersed or virtual working, cultural differences, people joining or leaving, scarce resources and pressure on wellbeing all make the team harder to develop. Co-location is the opposite: it helps.

test.q: Which of the following would make developing a project team EASIER rather than harder?
options: A wide spread of different time zones
test.why: Co-location makes communication and trust easier, so it is an enabler.

whyNot.0: Time zones make communication and meetings harder.
whyNot.3: Scarce resources create competing demands on people's time.
